messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Margaret, a 65-year-old retired military medic, still carried the weight of the accident that had nearly killed her four years ago. She had been riding in the back of a Humvee during a routine convoy, returning from a clinic, when a civilian sedan blew through a checkpoint and T-boned their vehicle at full speed. The impact threw her against the armored door; she felt ribs crack as the world went white. In the chaos that followed, she crawled to the driver, a young soldier whose leg was pinned, and tried to stem the bleeding while he screamed. She could still feel the slickness of blood on her hands, the smell of gasoline and hot metal, the way her own voice had sounded thin and far away when she called for help that seemed to take forever. The memory did not simply return—it seized her fully. When something brought it to mind, she would be back in that Humvee, the panic flooding her chest, the scene unfolding around her as if time had collapsed. The feeling overwhelmed every thought, and often she could not speak about it at all; the words were there but refused to form, and she would just shake her head and turn away.

In the months that followed, Margaret became acutely aware that certain things could trigger that reliving. The shape of a specific model of sedan—the same year and color as the one that had hit them—made her stomach clench. Even an image of any car crash on television was enough to send a shock through her. She began to feel uncomfortable in her own skin, a vague sense of wrongness that she could not name but that made her want to retreat. And the triggers set off a powerful threat response. When she saw a car that reminded her of the one that hit them, her body went on high alert: her shoulders tightened, her jaw locked, and she found herself scanning the road for danger. She became hyper-alert to unexpected or loud sounds—a car backfiring, a dropped pan—as though each noise might herald another impact. Her muscles stayed tense even at home.

The constant threat drained her. To cope, Margaret developed strategies to dampen the fear. She would eat excessively—snacks, leftovers, anything—to fill the hollow feeling that followed a trigger. She distracted herself with the television, flipping channels until her mind went numb. Most of all, she tried hard not to think about the accident, pushing away any memory that surfaced. But these strategies backfired. Suppressing her thoughts made her more sensitive to reminders; a glimpse of a sedan on the street now became an obsession, because her mind was working so hard to avoid it. And the overeating left her feeling sluggish and physically uncomfortable, which in turn kept her body on edge. The distraction rarely lasted; once the TV was off, the intrusive images returned with renewed force. So the threat level ratcheted up again, and she reached for more numbing behaviors, tightening the cycle.

Eventually, Margaret stopped driving altogether. She asked her neighbor to take her to the grocery store, and she avoided any street where she might encounter a similar sedan. Her daily life shrank to a few rooms. The weight of constant vigilance exhausted her, and the overeating had left her with high blood pressure and a lingering shame. She had come to believe that if she let her guard down, she might be caught unprepared again—that the accident had proven the world was unsafe. What frightened her most was not the memory itself but the feeling that she could not trust her own body to stay calm. She finally sought help after her daughter, calling from across the country, told her that she sounded scared on the phone. Margaret did not want to be scared anymore. She wanted to find a way to remember what happened without reliving it, and to feel safe in a world that still contained sedans.
